newsitem.title: USA: Clinton cites Hong Kong in defending China trade.
newsitem.headline: Clinton cites Hong Kong in defending China trade.

text.p: With the turnover of Hong Kong a few weeks away, President Bill Clinton on Saturday stepped up his effort to preserve most-favored-nation trade status for China, calling it a vital policy for the longtime British colony.

Fighting a powerful congressional drive to strip U.S. tariff relief from Beijing because of alleged human rights violations, persecution of religion and other misdeeds, Clinton used his five-minute weekly radio speech to try to rally the public to his side.

At the same time, the White House released a letter endorsed by every living former Treasury Secretary, Republican and Democrat, urging renewal of MFN for China. It also released a letter to Clinton from Chris Patten, the outgoing British governor of Hong Kong, urging the same thing.

"No-one is more concerned about human rights in China than the people of Hong Kong. But our strong view is that withdrawing or conditioning China's MFN status would not help to improve the human rights situation there," Patten wrote.

He added that denying China unconditional MFN renewal "would do great damage to Hong Kong's economy at the most sensitive time in its history. We estimate it would cost the territory 85,000 jobs and halve our GDP (Gross Domestic Product) growth," Patten said.

Hong Kong reverts to Chinese sovereignty on July 1 after nearly a century of British rule. In his radio speech, recorded at the White House on Friday before he departed for California to deliver a major address on race relations, Clinton reaffirmed U.S. policy on the transition -- that the people of Hong Kong must be allowed to retain their political freedom and an open economy.

"One thing we must not do is take any measures that would weaken Hong Kong just when it most needs to be strong and free," Clinton said. "No step would more clearly harm Hong Kong than reversing the course we have followed for years by denying normal trading status to China."

Congress is expected to try to overturn Clinton's decision to extend China's MFN status for another year before it begins its summer vacation in August. Clinton could veto a vote to reverse him, but Congress could prevail in the policy struggle by mustering a two-thirds majority in the Senate and House of Representatives.

Clinton said that the United States has a big economic interest in a smooth transition in Hong Kong because more than 1100 U.S. firms operate there, "making it the heart of American business in the fastest-growing part of the world."
